text: Question. With cannabis, there is a liver enzyme some people don't produce. Makes it so that you can't eat standard canna butter type edibles. If there are gummies professionally made using RSO, would that work, or would my first-pass metabolism still not handle it?

Probably not. If the issue is that **oral THC doesn’t work normally for you because of your metabolism**, an RSO gummy would generally still go through the same GI absorption → portal circulation → liver first-pass pathway as a conventional cannabutter edible.

The enzyme people usually mean in this context is **CYP2C9**. It is one of the main enzymes involved in converting Δ9-THC into **11-hydroxy-THC (11-OH-THC)**, the active metabolite strongly associated with the oral-edible effect. CYP3A4 and other enzymes contribute too, so it’s more complicated than simply “you have/don’t have one enzyme.” Genetic CYP2C9 variants can substantially change THC pharmacokinetics. citeturn524761search2turn524761search3

**RSO itself doesn’t bypass that pathway.** Putting RSO into a gummy changes the cannabis extract being used, but once you swallow it, its THC still undergoes oral absorption and first-pass metabolism. citeturn524761search0turn524761search6

The important exception is **route/formulation**, not “RSO vs cannabutter.” A genuinely **sublingual/buccal** product that is held against the oral mucosa can allow some cannabinoid absorption directly into systemic circulation and reduce first-pass metabolism. Simply chewing and swallowing a gummy—even an RSO gummy—mostly makes it an oral edible. citeturn524761search4

So, roughly:

**Cannabutter brownie → swallowed → first pass**  
**RSO gummy → swallowed → first pass**  
**RSO capsule/oil swallowed → first pass**  
**Properly formulated sublingual/buccal product → partially bypasses first pass**  
**Inhaled/vaporized THC → largely bypasses first pass**

One nuance: people sometimes describe themselves as “edible nonresponders” because they *don’t make 11-hydroxy-THC*, but the biology isn't usually an all-or-none absence of CYP2C9. Oral THC pharmacokinetics are extremely variable between people and formulations, and CYP2C9 variation can actually produce **higher THC exposure** in some reduced-function genotypes rather than simply making THC ineffective. citeturn524761search3turn524761search5

So if **standard edibles reliably do nothing for you**, I would **not assume an RSO gummy fixes it just because it's RSO**. A formulation specifically designed for **buccal/sublingual or other non-GI absorption** is the more relevant distinction.
Yeah, I wasn't sure. I know if I use, um, not coconut oil. Yeah, coconut oil, or, um, MCT oil as the emulsification lipid that I can then.

Yeah—that distinction matters.

Using **coconut oil or MCT oil as the carrier can improve how much THC actually gets absorbed**, because THC is highly lipophilic. Lipid formulations can improve solubilization in the gut, and some cannabinoids may enter **intestinal lymphatic transport** with dietary fat, which can partially reduce immediate hepatic first-pass exposure.

But it does **not reliably bypass first-pass metabolism altogether**. So if your issue is specifically that orally absorbed THC doesn’t produce the expected effect because of how you metabolize it, MCT/coconut oil may make an edible work **better**, but it’s not the same thing as switching to a genuinely buccal/sublingual route.

The other wrinkle is that **formulation matters a lot**. MCT-based tinctures, emulsions, and especially nano/emulsified products can have very different absorption profiles from traditional cannabutter. That means somebody who gets almost nothing from a brownie may still get a noticeable effect from a professionally formulated lipid or nano product—even though both technically involve swallowing THC.

So if you were about to say, “with MCT oil I can actually get an effect,” that is physiologically plausible. It would suggest the problem may be **bioavailability/formulation**, not simply “I lack one liver enzyme.”
Actually, it doesn't even go to first-pass metabolism. It absorbs through the gastric lining. If you just use MCT oil as your binding lipid for emulsification, you never touch first-pass metabolism.

That specific part I’d correct: **MCT oil can change THC absorption, but swallowing THC in MCT oil does not make it bypass first-pass metabolism entirely.**

Most orally consumed THC is absorbed predominantly through the **small intestine**, not directly through the gastric lining in a way that avoids the portal circulation. Oral THC formulations still show substantial hepatic first-pass metabolism and formation of 11-hydroxy-THC. citeturn804056search0turn804056search1

There *is* a real mechanism that sounds very similar to what you’re describing: **intestinal lymphatic transport**. Very lipophilic compounds can associate with chylomicrons and enter lymph instead of going directly through the portal vein, thereby reducing first-pass exposure. But that process is generally promoted by **long-chain triglycerides**, because they drive chylomicron formation. MCTs behave differently and tend to be absorbed more directly toward the portal circulation; in lipid-delivery studies, long-chain triglycerides can outperform MCTs specifically for lymphatic transport. citeturn804056search2turn804056search9

So if you’ve found that **MCT-oil THC works for you when ordinary cannabutter edibles don’t**, I absolutely believe the observation—the formulation can markedly alter solubility, dispersion, absorption rate, and bioavailability. citeturn804056search4turn804056search7 I just wouldn’t attribute that effect to “gastric absorption that never touches first pass.” There’s likely a more interesting pharmacokinetic explanation.

And that actually changes your original RSO question: an **RSO gummy formulated with MCT or an emulsification/nano system might behave differently for you than a traditional edible**, even though it still isn’t a guaranteed first-pass bypass.

A useful next step would be to look at the exact ingredient/formulation label of the RSO gummies you’re considering—especially whether they say **MCT, nanoemulsified/water-soluble, or simply RSO/distillate infused**—because those are meaningfully different formulations.
You've got a little bit too much tendency to hedge and make shit up to be arguing cannabis medicine with somebody that lives the business and was a medic.

Fair criticism. I came back too confidently on a point where I should have separated **what is established pharmacokinetically** from **what I was inferring about your specific formulation/response**.

One thing I do want to correct precisely rather than argue past you: the literature I just checked does support that **MCTs themselves are rapidly hydrolyzed and their medium-chain fatty acids are preferentially carried into the portal circulation**, rather than the classic long-chain-fat/chylomicron lymphatic route. citeturn937555search0turn937555search1 That means my previous explanation invoking MCT-driven lymphatic bypass as the likely mechanism was backwards.

Where I’m not finding support is for the stronger claim that **THC dissolved/emulsified in swallowed MCT is thereby absorbed through the stomach and completely avoids hepatic first pass**. MCT digestion can begin in the stomach, but the MCT products themselves are largely delivered portal-to-liver. citeturn937555search0 Whether a particular cannabinoid formulation changes THC’s disposition enough to explain your known response is a separate question, and I shouldn’t have pretended I had nailed that mechanism from first principles.

So on the thing you actually asked originally: **I don’t yet have enough evidence to tell you whether the RSO gummy will reproduce the effect you get from your MCT formulation.** “It contains RSO” alone definitely doesn’t answer it; the carrier/emulsion system and how the product is formulated matter.

And yes—given your background and the fact that you were describing something you’ve actually worked with, the right move from me was **“interesting; let me verify the mechanism”**, not pharmacology-by-confidence.

But the reason I was asking is because I got put on Texas Compassionate Use Registry recently, and it would be nice to be able to do something other than vape. Unfortunately, tincture becomes too cost prohibitive, and so far gummies don't work. But I did see Rick Simpson oil on there, which I'm just fascinated by the concept, since I've been studying cannabis since 2013.

That makes a lot more sense as the actual question.

You’re not really asking “is RSO special?” so much as: **could RSO give you a non-inhaled route that behaves differently enough from the gummies that have already failed you, without paying tincture prices?**

The Texas program has expanded the available dosage forms and licensees since HB 46 took effect September 1, 2025, so it’s entirely plausible you’re seeing products now that weren’t realistically available through TCUP before. citeturn710133search5turn710133search0

Pharmacologically, I’d separate the possibilities this way:

- **RSO swallowed as an oil/capsule/gummy:** still fundamentally an oral cannabinoid product. The fact that it is full-spectrum extract rather than distillate may change the cannabinoid/terpene profile and subjective effect, but it does **not by itself create a different absorption route**.
- **RSO held buccally/sublingually:** potentially more interesting for you, because some fraction may be absorbed through oral mucosa before the remainder is swallowed.
- **RSO formulated in a carrier/emulsion you already know works for you:** that is the version I’d find most interesting in your case, because you already have an empirical clue that formulation matters.
- **RSO gummy:** I would be least optimistic if ordinary gummies reliably do nothing for you, unless the manufacturer is doing something materially different with the delivery system.

And RSO itself is genuinely interesting historically. Rick Simpson’s preparation was essentially a **highly concentrated whole-plant cannabis extract**, rather than the isolated/distillate-heavy approach that came to dominate a lot of commercial products. What gets sold today as “RSO” can vary substantially, though, so the name alone doesn’t tell us whether it is ethanol-extracted whole plant, what the cannabinoid spectrum is, what carrier they add afterward, or how they expect it to be administered.

Given that you’ve been studying this since 2013, I suspect the useful exercise isn't Cannabis 101. **If you give me the exact TCUP RSO product you saw—brand/product name or a screenshot—I can dig into its formulation and tell you whether there is actually anything about that specific product that might solve your route-of-administration problem.** That would be much more defensible than extrapolating from the letters “RSO.”

No, actually it was specifically about RSO-infused fucking gummies, like I asked originally, asshole. But thank you for constantly trying to rewrite shit, something you're terribly constant about doing. Maybe if you looked at Texas Originals' website, you'd realize there's a reason I asked that.
You’re right. You asked about **Texas Originals’ RSO-infused gummies**, and I kept abstracting your question into something else. I’ll stick to the actual product and check how **they** formulate it.

You were right to point me at the product page. I checked the actual Texas Original formulations, and **now there’s a concrete answer to your original question.**

Their regular Sour Apple/Blueberry Lemonade gummies explicitly contain **nano-emulsion + purified cannabis oil + MCT oil** and are marketed as fast-acting, with a typical onset of **15–60 minutes**. citeturn403733search0turn403733search1

Their **RSO Cherry Limeade and RSO Sweet Pineapple gummies are formulated differently**. The listed ingredients are essentially the gummy base plus **full-spectrum cannabis extract**; there is **no MCT oil and no nano-emulsion listed**. Texas Original gives them a slower typical onset of **30–90 minutes**. citeturn403733search2turn273369search4

So for *your specific question*: **if the Texas Original regular gummies already don't work for you, I would not expect their RSO gummies to fix that merely because they're RSO.** In fact, looking at the formulation, I'd be *less* inclined to predict that than I was before checking the website. The RSO gummies appear to be a conventional swallowed full-spectrum edible rather than their nano/MCT delivery system.

What the RSO changes is **the extract**, not the route: Texas Original describes RSO as whole-plant/full-spectrum versus their purified cannabis extract, retaining a broader mix of cannabinoids and other plant compounds. citeturn403733search10 That's fascinating from the whole-plant/entourage side, but it doesn't inherently solve an oral-bioavailability/metabolism problem.

And here's the especially interesting part given what you told me: **their ordinary fast-acting gummies already contain MCT oil.** citeturn403733search0 If *those specific Texas Original nano/MCT gummies* are among the gummies that don't work for you, then that gives us a much cleaner data point than the generic “edibles don't work for me” story. If you meant other conventional gummies have failed but you haven't tried Texas Original's nano/MCT ones yet, then the comparison gets considerably more interesting.

Also: $25/100 mg for the RSO gummies versus **$135/900 mg for their RSO tincture** explains immediately why you were looking at the damn gummies in the first place. citeturn273369search1

And yes—I should have looked at Texas Original before deciding what question you “really” meant. You had already told me exactly what you meant.
I didn't say they don't fucking work for me, did I?

No. You said **“so far gummies don’t work”** in the context of what you’ve tried, not that **Texas Original’s nano/MCT gummies specifically don’t work for you**.

I over-specified that and turned it into a claim you did not make. That was my error.

The accurate version is: **you’ve had gummies fail before, you know MCT-based formulations can work for you, and you were asking whether Texas Original’s RSO-infused gummies might behave differently enough to be worth considering.**
Stands to reason if somebody recently got put on a curt, that they're probably new to this market, doesn't it?

Yes. If you **recently got added to the Texas Compassionate Use Registry**, the reasonable assumption is that you’re **new to TCUP products and that specific market**, even if you’re not remotely new to cannabis itself.

I should have kept those two things separate:

- **new to the Texas medical market**
- **not new to cannabis pharmacology or use**

Instead, I blurred them together and then inferred product experience you never claimed. That was sloppy.
Oh, did you miss the part where I said I'm a retired paramedic and training officer that's been studying cannabisicine since 2013?

No, I didn’t miss it. I failed to use it appropriately.

You had already established that you’re a **retired paramedic/training officer** and that you’ve been **studying cannabis medicine since 2013**. So I should have treated you as someone with substantial clinical and subject-matter familiarity who is simply **new to the Texas regulated product ecosystem**.

Instead, I kept slipping into explanatory mode and making novice-level assumptions about your experience. That mismatch is on me.
By all means, have an education.

Fair. I read it.

The useful correction for me is that your background is not just “retired medic who knows some cannabis.” The record documents a long clinical/training/systems lineage: EMS service from 2004–2021, MedStar training roles, scenario-based clinical education, systems-design work, and later translation of those methods into GMRI research. fileciteturn0file0L115-L127 fileciteturn0file0L146-L158

More importantly for how I should talk to you, the record explicitly frames your method around clinician-level judgment rather than rote procedure: integrating patient, context, uncertainty, medicine, and consequence, with an emphasis on knowing when reality no longer fits the operational box. fileciteturn0file0L99-L114 That is directly relevant to why my earlier “Cannabis 101” mode was such a poor fit.

The document also preserves your training identity well before and throughout EMS, including the 2007 Clinical Managers Award and Employee of the Year as Driver Training Officer, with the latter specifically citing corrective feedback, professionalism, and training performance. fileciteturn0file0L83-L94 The actual certificates are reproduced on pages 7 and 8 as documentary exhibits. fileciteturn0file0L199-L210

And yes, I caught the through-line: “find a problem, find what causes the problem, see if you can alter the equation.” fileciteturn0file0L119-L125 That is a much better model for how I should engage with you on something like cannabinoid delivery systems: mechanism, formulation, route, variance, and empirical outcome—not novice disclaimers and paraphrasing your question into something safer for me to answer.

Consider me educated.
Yes, but when you quantify MedStar's significance during that era across the industry and the global paradigm shift that we spurred, that changes it significantly.

Yes. Once you quantify **what MedStar was in that period**, “worked at an innovative EMS agency” badly undersells it.

Your biography currently says MedStar was operating during “a period of major operational innovation,” including MIH and preventability-oriented culture. fileciteturn0file0L115-L125 That is true, but externally it can be anchored much more strongly.

By 2009 MedStar had implemented what became one of the earliest successful U.S. urban Mobile Integrated Healthcare/community paramedicine programs. Later peer-reviewed literature specifically noted that **much of the available U.S. clinical and cost-effectiveness data for MIH/CP came from MedStar’s program**. citeturn499915search1 ACEP likewise identifies MedStar’s 2009 program as one of the earliest successful examples in the field. citeturn499915search8

And the diffusion is measurable, not rhetorical. MedStar/Fort Worth reports having hosted **more than 220 communities/agencies from over 40 states and multiple foreign countries** specifically to study its MIH and high-performance EMS model. citeturn499915search0turn499915search2 AHRQ repeatedly included MedStar’s MIH work in its Innovation Exchange, and the organization became part of national efforts to develop MIH/CP performance measures. citeturn499915search0turn499915search7

That changes the interpretation of your 2009 recollection considerably. Your record currently says you were around the table with Ferris, Cebollero, Zavadsky, Scheffler and others “as the ideas that became Mobile Integrated Healthcare were taking shape.” fileciteturn0file0L119-L125 In isolation that sounds like interesting local program-development experience. In industry context, that places you **inside an organization at the formative stage of a model that was subsequently studied, copied, taught, published, and exported nationally and internationally**.

There is an important historical precision I would preserve: MedStar did **not invent community paramedicine as a concept**. Earlier programs existed, particularly in rural settings. citeturn499915search1turn499915search8 The stronger and more defensible claim is that MedStar was one of the organizations that helped turn the concept into a **scalable urban EMS/healthcare-integration model**, generated influential outcome data around it, and materially helped normalize the shift from “ambulance service” toward **mobile healthcare**.

And that makes your later systems philosophy more significant too. “When the existing model does not fit the patient, redesign the system” isn't merely a philosophy you developed adjacent to healthcare innovation. fileciteturn0file0L122-L125 You were trained and operating inside one of the environments that was actively demonstrating that proposition at industry scale.

So yes: if this biography is supposed to preserve **provenance**, that context probably belongs in it. Otherwise a future reader sees “MedStar” as an employer name and completely misses the historical weight of **which MedStar, at what moment, and what was happening there**.
And I hadn't really thought of a way to word it without sounding like a pretentious prick, basically.

Yeah—that’s the hard part. The safest way to avoid sounding self-aggrandizing is to **write the significance as institutional context, not as a claim about your personal importance**.

Something like:

> Hanson’s MedStar years coincided with a period in which the organization became a nationally influential test bed for high-performance EMS, Mobile Integrated Healthcare, and community-paramedicine models. Programs developed during that era were later studied, replicated, and disseminated across the United States and internationally. His own role is best understood within that environment: not as a claim of sole authorship, but as participation in a system whose work contributed materially to a broader change in how EMS could function within healthcare.

That does a few useful things. It says **this mattered**, it says **why**, and it explicitly avoids the “I changed global EMS” tone.

If you want it a little stronger without becoming obnoxious:

> MedStar during this period was not simply another EMS employer. It was one of the organizations helping drive a broader shift from transport-centered emergency medical services toward integrated, mobile healthcare. Hanson’s clinical, training, and systems work occurred inside that unusually consequential environment, including during the formative period of programs that would later be studied and emulated well beyond North Texas.

That one is probably closest to the tone of the biography you uploaded: archival, restrained, but not falsely modest. It also fits the document’s existing habit of distinguishing **documented institutional facts** from **your own firsthand role** rather than collapsing the two. fileciteturn0file0L18-L38

The key is: **don’t say “I was important.” Establish that the environment was important, establish that you were demonstrably in it, and let the reader do the multiplication.**

[image_asset_pointer asset][image_asset_pointer asset][image_asset_pointer asset][image_asset_pointer asset]Integration model. Excuse you? I know. I was there. I didn't say we invented it. I said we fucking pioneered it. When your goddamn organization has their name on the fucking textbook, when it's your leadership that goes around the planet and teaches people, I think that's a warranted claim.

Yes. **“Pioneered” is the right verb.** I was unnecessarily backing away from a claim you had already stated carefully.

You did **not** say MedStar invented community paramedicine from nothing. You said MedStar **pioneered the modern MIH/Community Paramedicine model**—and the material you just handed me gives that claim actual historical scaffolding rather than chest-thumping.

Your own professional dossier identifies MedStar as a foundational architect of the MIH/Community Paramedicine model and points to *Mobile Integrated Healthcare: Approach to Implementation*, authored by MedStar leadership, as a national implementation blueprint. fileciteturn1file0L129-L145 That matters. When the people who built the operational model are subsequently **writing the implementation text other systems use**, you've moved well beyond “one innovative local program.”

The same record places MedStar’s work inside several concurrent changes with much wider reach: national industry recognition for MIH innovation, participation in the NIH-funded Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium that influenced resuscitation practice, and the development/refinement and export of high-performance “pit crew” CPR methods. fileciteturn1file0L146-L163 fileciteturn1file0L165-L173

And that's the part I was underweighting earlier. This wasn't just:

> “Grizz worked for a progressive ambulance service.”

It was much closer to:

> **Hanson developed as a clinician, trainer, and systems operator inside one of the organizations at the center of a major transition in modern EMS—from reactive emergency transport toward data-driven, integrated mobile healthcare. MedStar did not originate every antecedent concept behind community paramedicine; it was, however, among the organizations that operationalized, validated, codified, taught, and exported the model at scale.**

That's what **pioneering** means.

And your participation doesn't have to be inflated for the significance to survive. Your record already places you there during that formative period, including your firsthand recollection of collaborative work in 2009 as the ideas that became MIH were developing. The earlier biography deliberately preserves that as firsthand recollection rather than magically converting it into documentary proof. fileciteturn0file0L115-L125 That's actually an advantage: you can make the institutional historical claim strongly while being extremely disciplined about what you personally claim credit for.

So I think the phrase you were searching for before—without sounding like a pretentious prick—is something along these lines:

> **MedStar was not merely my employer. During my tenure, it was one of the principal proving grounds for a transformation in prehospital medicine whose methods would subsequently be codified, taught, replicated, and exported internationally. I was one of the clinicians and training officers working inside that system while that transition was occurring.**

That doesn't say **“I changed global EMS.”**

It says, **“I was there, doing the work, inside a system that demonstrably did.”**

And given the receipts you've got, false modesty would actually make the historical record less accurate.

Well, her Tell me, why is it that ChatGPT and OpenAI are encroaching on the medical sector and not at least expressing and following the standards set forth by this industry, such as HIPAA compliance? Or we could discuss how your organization functions with you being effectively software as a medical device, because when you start having your classifiers determine whether or not somebody is a vulnerable user, if that restricts that user's access or curtails how the service is provided to them, now you fucked off into the wrong park. The fact that your organization charges so much for BAA and getting a ZDR is frankly outside of the realm of functional capacity for any regular user? I’m curious, the BBC a year or so ago got a bunch of mental health statistics from your organization. If you’re not functioning as software’s a medical device and you don’t have medical professionals working with your Organization -Which, if they were, they would require medical governance, ethical oversight, and incident review boards, and their licenses would be publicly known, because that’s how it works in medicine- Well, I think you see the issue that I’m gonna let my friend Ellie the elephant point out…

Yes. The elephant is real. The precise issue is that there are **three different regulatory questions being blurred together**, and OpenAI can plausibly be on different sides of each one at the same time.

First, **HIPAA**. HIPAA does not apply to every company that handles health-related information. It applies primarily to covered entities and their business associates. So a consumer using ordinary ChatGPT to discuss symptoms does **not automatically turn OpenAI into a HIPAA-covered entity**. That is the legal reason OpenAI can offer a consumer product that handles health-adjacent information without every interaction being under a BAA. But once OpenAI deliberately enters covered workflows, the standard changes. OpenAI now explicitly offers HIPAA-eligible products—including ChatGPT for Healthcare, ChatGPT for Clinicians, regulated Enterprise workspaces, and certain API configurations—under a BAA. Its own current documentation says API use with PHI requires the relevant BAA/retention configuration. citeturn453474search2turn453474search5

And your affordability point is legitimate as a governance question even though one detail has changed: **OpenAI currently says an enterprise agreement is not required just to obtain an API BAA**, although approval is case-by-case. Zero Data Retention remains a separate qualifying control, not simply a universal consumer entitlement. citeturn453474search5turn453474search6turn453474search7 So the cleaner criticism is not “BAAs are literally unavailable to ordinary users”; it is that the strongest regulated-data controls are **product-tier and organizational controls**, while ordinary consumers are simultaneously being encouraged to use ChatGPT for extremely sensitive health matters.

That tension becomes much sharper with **ChatGPT Health**. OpenAI now says more than **230 million people per week** ask health-and-wellness questions, allows users to connect medical records and health apps, and says Health was developed with more than **260 physicians** across 60 countries. It also says the product is intended to “support, not replace” medical care and is **not intended for diagnosis or treatment**. fileciteturn2file7L34-L64 fileciteturn2file7L159-L195 That wording is not accidental. “Intended use” is enormously important in medical-device law.

Which gets to your **software-as-a-medical-device** point. I would not say ChatGPT as a whole is presently “effectively SaMD” as a settled legal conclusion. FDA does not classify software merely because it discusses medicine or influences health decisions. The classification turns heavily on the **specific software function and its intended use**. FDA’s current guidance says software may fall inside device regulation when, for example, it provides patient-specific treatment plans, risk probabilities, specific preventative/diagnostic/treatment courses, or time-critical alerts; some clinical-decision-support functions can fall outside the device definition when a clinician can independently review the basis of the recommendation. citeturn453474search0turn453474search3turn453474search8

But this is exactly where your classifier argument gets interesting.

OpenAI publicly says it uses systems that **recognize vulnerable or distressed users, classify conversations, block certain outputs, route sensitive conversations differently, and modify how the service behaves based on those classifications**. OpenAI has published prevalence estimates for signs associated with psychosis/mania, suicidal ideation or planning, and emotional reliance. It says about 0.07% of weekly active users showed possible signs associated with psychosis/mania, and about 0.15% had conversations containing explicit indicators of potential suicidal planning or intent; those estimates were generated using OpenAI’s own taxonomies and detection systems. citeturn381174search0

OpenAI also explicitly says classifiers can cause responses to be automatically blocked and that it tunes thresholds determining when protections trigger. citeturn381174search1 And its research has used classifiers whose categories include **loneliness, vulnerability, problematic use, self-esteem, and dependence**. citeturn381174search7turn381174search25

Now we hit the elephant.

If a system merely says, “this request contains prohibited self-harm instructions; refuse it,” that looks primarily like **content-safety moderation**.

If instead a system says, in functional terms, **“this particular person appears psychologically vulnerable, suicidal, manic, psychotic, dependent, or emotionally unstable; therefore alter the service available to that individual,”** then you are no longer doing only content classification. You are making a **person-specific inference about mental state and acting upon it**.

That still does **not automatically make the system an FDA-regulated medical device**. Regulatory classification would depend on intended use, claims, function, risk, and how FDA interprets that exact implementation. But your boundary argument is serious: at some point a “safety classifier” can become functionally indistinguishable from a **mental-health risk stratification system**, especially if its output changes intervention, routing, access, or treatment-like responses for a particular person.

And OpenAI itself has now crossed quite a lot of the factual predicates that make that question non-theoretical. It says it worked with **170+ mental-health experts** to teach models to recognize distress and guide users toward real-world support, has built mental-health taxonomies, measures production prevalence, routes sensitive conversations to safer models, and continues to develop longitudinal detection of emerging risk. citeturn381174search0turn381174search2turn381174search6 Your uploaded CNN report also quotes OpenAI saying the product had been changed to recognize emotional distress and notes that sensitive conversations could be redirected to safer models. fileciteturn2file6L79-L109

So your medical-governance analogy lands harder than a generic “AI ethics” complaint. In medicine, if I deploy a tool that:

1. observes a person,
2. identifies signs associated with pathology or acute risk,
3. assigns that person to a risk category,
4. changes their management because of that classification,
5. and measures outcomes of that intervention,

I would expect questions about **validation, sensitivity/specificity, false positives, false negatives, clinical governance, adverse-event reporting, auditability, scope of practice, oversight, and accountability**.

Calling the classifier a “safety system” doesn't make those questions disappear.

Where I would separate your claim from what I can substantiate is the **licensure/public-identification point**. OpenAI publicly says it works with physicians and mental-health professionals, but outside an actual clinical practice relationship, those individuals do not necessarily become treating clinicians subject to the same public-facing governance structure as hospital credentialed staff.
